questions.question: The true dividing line between rural and urban settlements is:
options: The dominant economic activity — primary for rural, secondary and tertiary for urban

questions.question: A description that mentions relief, drainage, soil, water supply and aspect is describing a settlement's:
options: Site — the physical character of the exact ground it stands on

questions.question: A Namaqualand farmstead pressed close around its borehole illustrates:
options: A wet-point site — chosen because water is available exactly there in a dry region
A nucleated village on communal land

subtopics.title: Classifying Settlements: Size, Pattern and Function

questions.question: The correct ascending order of the settlement ladder is:
options: Village, farmstead, hamlet, town, metropolis, city
Hamlet, farmstead, village, city, town, metropolis
Farmstead, village, hamlet, town, city, metropolis
Farmstead, hamlet, village, town, city, metropolis

questions.question: Dispersed rural settlement is typically explained by:
options: Communal land ownership around a shared water point
Large, privately owned farms on which each farmer must live
The pull of a road junction

questions.question: Nucleated settlement clusters dwellings around a central point because of:
options: Communal tenure, defence, shared water and community life

questions.question: A rural settlement is described as unifunctional because:
options: One dominant activity, almost always tied to the land, supports it
It offers every kind of service

subtopics.title: Rural Shapes: Round, Linear, T-Shaped and Crossroad

questions.question: Dwellings arranged in a circle around a central cattle kraal form a:
options: Round village, built for defence and community life

questions.question: A linear village grows long and thin because:
options: Every household wants frontage on the road or river it follows
The soil is only fertile in a line
The wind blows along one axis

questions.question: The difference between a T-shaped and a crossroad village is that:
options: The T-shape follows a river while the crossroad follows a ridge
In the T-shape a side road ends against the main road; in the crossroad two roads intersect and buildings take all four arms
The crossroad form has no shops

questions.question: Junction settlements exist because a junction:
options: Concentrates passing trade where traffic slows, stops and turns

subtopics.title: Rural Functions and Land Use: Why the Settlement Is There

questions.question: Extensive stock farming, as in the Karoo, produces:
options: Homesteads spaced enormously far apart, because each family needs thousands of hectares

questions.question: A plantation village in the timber country of the escarpment exists to:
options: House the teams who plant, thin and fell the planted forests, near a sawmill settlement

questions.question: Staff villages and rest camps inside a park such as Addo Elephant National Park serve the function of:
options: Conservation — managing protected land and hosting its visitors

questions.question: The five-move commentary on a rural settlement covers:
options: Rainfall, temperature, wind, soil and altitude
Population, language, income, transport and history
Classification, pattern with reason, shape with cause, function from land use, and site and situation
Name, province, district, municipality and ward

subtopics.title: The Stand and the Street: Site versus Situation

questions.question: Asking whether storm water ponds against the wall and whether winter sun reaches the kitchen belongs to the conversation about:
options: Site — the exact patch of earth under the building
Situation — the house among its surroundings

questions.question: Asking how far the house lies from the school, the clinic and the taxi rank belongs to:
options: Situation — position relative to everything around it

questions.question: Homes on the dry shelf above a flood-prone valley floor, with fields on the wet flats below, show:
options: A dry-point site — chosen to escape the water while still using it

subtopics.title: Scattered Mealies or One Pot: Dispersed and Nucleated

questions.question: In the beans picture, beans flung across the floor represent:
options: Dispersed settlement — homesteads far apart on large private farms

questions.question: Beans poured into one bowl represent nucleated settlement, whose classic South African setting is:
options: Villages on communal land, where people live together and walk out to the fields
Commercial wheat farms of the Swartland

questions.question: The reason-mark linking pattern to ownership is:
options: Scattered pattern follows shared land; clustered follows private land
Scattered pattern follows private land; clustered pattern follows shared, communal land
Both patterns follow soil fertility only

questions.question: Each step up the settlement ladder adds:
options: More people and more services together

subtopics.title: Reading a Village Like a Taxi Route

questions.question: A long, thin settlement with every building facing the road is named and explained as:
options: Linear — frontage on the routeway that flows past

questions.question: The 'junction is a magnet' idea means:
options: Where traffic slows and turns, sellers set up and homes follow along the arms

questions.question: Dark, ruler-straight rows of planted pine and gum around a village indicate the function of:
options: Forestry — serving the plantations and the sawmill

questions.question: The density rule for farming settlements states that:
options: All farming settlements have the same density
Extensive farming packs homesteads close together
Intensive farming on small high-value plots supports closer settlement; extensive farming spreads homesteads far apart
